title: The Rented Theatre to the Sangre de Cristo: Graham, the Contraction, and the American Body
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Allegheny City and the Road West

stops.name: Allegheny City, the birth on the north bank
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The coordinate is Allegheny Center on Pittsburgh's North Side; Allegheny City was an independent municipality until Pittsburgh annexed it on 9 December 1907, and one summary of the birth gives a coordinate south of the rivers, in downtown Pittsburgh, outside the former city entirely
stops.campa: Martha Graham is born in Allegheny City, a municipality on the north bank that Pittsburgh will annex thirteen years later. Her father George Graham is an alienist, a practitioner of the early psychiatry that reads a patient's body for what the patient will not say. The household is strict Presbyterian and dancing is not among the things a daughter is raised toward. She will spend seventy years building an art on her father's working premise, that movement does not lie. No source reached records him saying it to her more than once.
suggested_refs: The Allegheny Center district of Pittsburgh's North Side, the former independent city of Allegheny

stops.name: Santa Maria, the family goes west
stops.date_confidence: the year rests on the phrase 'when Martha was fourteen' and the month is not attested. The town is contested and is left unresolved here: Wikipedia's 'Martha Graham' names Santa Maria, while Agnes de Mille's biography and Graham's own Blood Memory are read by most biographers as naming Santa Barbara, ninety miles down the same coast
stops.campa: The family leaves Pennsylvania for the California coast when Martha is fourteen, moving for air and climate as families of that decade did. The encyclopedia entry names Santa Maria; the standard biographies name Santa Barbara, ninety miles down the same coast, and the two towns have never been reconciled in print. Every account agrees on what the move changed. A Presbyterian childhood of closed interiors gives way to dry hills and a Pacific horizon with nothing built on it.
suggested_refs: The contested relocation town: Santa Maria in the encyclopedia record, Santa Barbara in the biographies
sources: Agnes de Mille, Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham (1991)

stops.name: Mason Opera House, Los Angeles: Ruth St. Denis on the stage
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month and day of the performance she attended are not established by any source reached
stops.campa: At the Mason Opera House on South Broadway, seventeen years old, she watches Ruth St. Denis dance. St. Denis performs an East assembled from postcards and temple photographs, incense and brass laid over borrowed gesture. Graham decides that evening on a life in dance, against her father's wish and against the whole arrangement of her upbringing. She will not begin training for five more years. She goes first to the Cumnock School, a junior college for young women with a program in dramatic expression.
suggested_refs: The Mason Opera House, 127 South Broadway, Los Angeles

stops.name: 600 St. Paul Avenue, Los Angeles: the Denishawn school
stops.date_confidence: Graham joins during the school's second summer, 1916; the month within that year is not attested. The school itself opened in the summer of 1915 as the Ruth St. Denis School of Dancing and Its Related Arts, so 1916 is her arrival and not the founding
stops.campa: Denishawn occupies a Spanish house on St. Paul Avenue above the city, where Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn teach ballet, yoga, Delsarte, and their own inventions to whoever pays. Graham arrives in the school's second summer, the year after it opens, and stays more than six years: first a pupil, then an instructor, then a teacher at the company's later quarters near Westlake Park. The training is theatrical and eclectic, borrowed from every continent at once. She takes all of it and spends the next decade getting free of it.
suggested_refs: The Denishawn house at 600 St. Paul Avenue, in the old Crown Hill district of Los Angeles

stops.name: Shubert Theatre, Manhattan: the Greenwich Village Follies
stops.date_confidence: she dances two seasons, 1923 to 1925; the month is not attested. The revue's name outlived its address: by these years the Greenwich Village Follies had left its namesake downtown theatre and opened in Broadway houses, so the venue pin is the Shubert rather than the Greenwich Village Theatre named in some summaries
stops.campa: She leaves Denishawn for New York and takes work as a featured dancer in the Greenwich Village Follies, a revue that had long since left Greenwich Village for the Broadway houses uptown. Two seasons of it pay her rent. The choreography is not hers and the audience is not there for her. Neither will be true of her again. Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn are three thousand miles behind her, and she is twenty-nine years old and has never yet put a dance of her own in front of anybody who paid to see it.
suggested_refs: The Greenwich Village Follies, 1923 and 1924 editions, in their uptown Broadway houses

stops.name: Eastman Theatre, Rochester: the first authority
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is dated to 1925; the month is not attested. The theatre on Gibbs Street had opened on 4 September 1922, so it is not new in the year she arrives
stops.campa: George Eastman's theatre on Gibbs Street has been open three years when Graham is hired to run dance instruction at the school attached to it. Rouben Mamoulian directs there, years before Hollywood. The post is salaried and the room is hers to shape: her first authority over a company of dancers, in a city four hundred miles from both the Denishawn house and the Broadway revue that had been paying her. Here she begins working without the decorative vocabulary she was taught, and finds what is under it is breath under strain.
suggested_refs: The Eastman Theatre and Eastman School of Music, 26 Gibbs Street, Rochester

stops.name: Eastman School, Rochester: The Flute of Krishna
stops.date_confidence: the film is made at the Eastman School in 1926; the month is not attested. One summary of the life dates it to 1925 by conflating it with the Eastman appointment, which is a year earlier
stops.campa: Mamoulian films her students in The Flute of Krishna, a short dance piece shot at the Eastman School. The material is pure Denishawn, orientalist and costumed, and it survives, which most of what she makes in this decade does not. Four years earlier she had appeared in a silent film directed by Hugo Riesenfeld alongside the dancer Lillian Powell. The camera finds her twice before the stage does, and both times it records the work she is about to repudiate.
suggested_refs: The Flute of Krishna (1926), directed by Rouben Mamoulian at the Eastman School of Music

stops.name: 48th Street Theatre, Manhattan: the first independent concert
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of April she rents the 48th Street Theatre and gives a concert of eighteen short solos and trios, every one of them her own. She is thirty-two. The evening is the founding act of the Martha Graham Dance Company, which becomes the oldest dance company in America and outlives her by decades. Nothing on the programme yet announces the severity that is coming, and she says so herself. The break from Denishawn is a matter of ownership before it is a matter of style: her theatre, her rent, her name on the bill.
stops.quote: Everything I did was influenced by Denishawn.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham on her 1926 debut concert, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Martha Graham', footnote 12
suggested_refs: The 48th Street Theatre, Manhattan, site of the 18 April 1926 debut concert

stops.name: Carnegie Hall Studio 61, Manhattan: the school
stops.date_confidence: 1926, from the company's own history page; the month is not attested and the September anchor places the school after the April debut rather than before it
stops.campa: She rents a small studio in the Carnegie Hall complex and opens a school in it. The building is a warren of teachers above the concert hall: voice, piano, ballet, elocution, each in a rented room. Out of Studio 61 come the technique classes that turn contraction and release into a syllabus, the first American modern dance vocabulary that can be taught to strangers who have never seen her dance. The school outlasts the studio, and it outlasts the woman who opened it.
suggested_refs: Studio 61 of the Carnegie Hall studio towers, first home of the Graham school

stops.name: Klaw Theatre, Manhattan: the second recital
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Seven months after the first concert she gives another, at the Klaw Theatre on West 45th Street. There is no payroll and no subscription season, and no critic is obliged to be there. The recitals are self-produced and self-financed, and there will be twenty years more of them before an American audience for this work reliably exists. Louis Horst, who had been Denishawn's musical director, came east when she did and plays and composes for these programmes. He stays beside the work until his death.
suggested_refs: The Klaw Theatre, West 45th Street, site of the recital of 28 November 1926

stops.name: 340 East 54th Street, Manhattan: the Neighborhood Playhouse School
stops.date_confidence: the school's founding year, 1928, is attested; the month of her appointment is not. Some accounts place this stop on Grand Street on the Lower East Side, at the original Neighborhood Playhouse theatre, which had closed a year before the school existed
stops.campa: Alice and Irene Lewisohn open a school of the theatre on East 54th Street, and Graham joins the faculty in its first year, teaching movement to actors as well as to dancers. The old Neighborhood Playhouse on Grand Street, downtown, had closed the year before; the school keeps the name and none of the address. She teaches in this building for decades, and the actors who pass through the room carry her technique into a medium that never once names it on a credit.
suggested_refs: The Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre, 340 East 54th Street, founded 1928
sources: Wikipedia, 'Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre'

stops.name: New York, Heretic
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the premiere day is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Heretic sets one figure in white against a wall of women in black who will not let her through, danced to a single Breton folk song played over and over. There is no scenery and no ornament, and the costumes are tubes of jersey. Audiences accustomed to the incense and brass of Denishawn find the thing ugly and say so in print, and Graham does not soften it by a degree. She is thirty-five and has arrived at the subject she will work for sixty years: the single body pressed against the group that made it.
stops.quote: Frequently the vividness and intensity of her purpose are so potent that on the rise of the curtain they strike like a blow.
stops.quote_source: John Martin, dance critic of the New York Times, on Graham; the traceable printing is Merle Armitage, ed., Martha Graham (1937), p. 9, not a located Times review
suggested_refs: Heretic (1929), the earliest surviving statement of the Graham group vocabulary

stops.name: Chanin Theatre, Manhattan: Mary Wigman comes over
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Mary Wigman gives her first American performance at the Chanin Theatre, and Graham's whole generation is in the house. Wigman dances alone with a percussionist, in masks, out of a German expressionism she arrived at along a line parallel to Graham's and entirely separate from it. Her three American seasons and hundred and seventy performances are credited with making modern dance a two-shored art. Two women have solved the same problem on two continents, neither having needed the other's answer to do it.
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman's American debut, Chanin Theatre, 28 December 1930

stops.name: New York, the first Guggenheim in choreography
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month of the award is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: The Guggenheim Foundation gives her a fellowship in choreography, reportedly the first it has ever given a dancer. Two more will follow, in 1943 and 1944. The money is the first institutional statement that what she does is composition rather than performance. A dance can be written the way a symphony is written, except that the composer here is also the instrument being written for. She is thirty-eight years old and has been making her own work for six of them.
suggested_refs: The John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation fellowships of 1932, 1943 and 1944

stops.name: Bennington College, Vermont: the summer school
stops.date_confidence: the Bennington School of the Dance is founded in 1934; the exact opening date of the first summer session is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: The Bennington School of the Dance opens on a Vermont campus four years old, founded by Martha Hill, with Graham, Doris Humphrey, Hanya Holm, and Charles Weidman teaching inside the same six weeks. The four disagree about nearly everything a dance can be and are installed side by side regardless. Each summer the students go home and teach what they were given, in colleges and studios across the country, and within a decade the technique of a woman who cannot fill a New York theatre is the standard training of American dance.
suggested_refs: The Bennington School of the Dance, founded 1934 by Martha Hill on the Bennington College campus

stops.name: New York, Frontier and the first Noguchi set
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the premiere day is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Frontier is a solo: a section of rail fence, two ropes running back into the dark, and a woman claiming the ground in front of it. The set is by Isamu Noguchi, the first of a collaboration that runs thirty-five years. Noguchi gives her objects rather than scenery, things a dancer can stand on and be measured against, so that the stage acquires a geometry the body has to answer. The fence rail reads as the whole American West, and nobody in the theatre needs that explained.
suggested_refs: Frontier (1935), set by Isamu Noguchi, first of their collaborations

stops.name: New York, the refusal of Berlin
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the date of the letter declining the invitation is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Germany invites her company to the international dance festival attached to the Berlin Olympics. Graham declines in writing, and puts her reasons in the letter rather than pleading a scheduling conflict. Goebbels is reported to have written back assuring her that her Jewish dancers would receive complete immunity; only that fragment of the letter has been seen, and the full text is not accessible here. Several of her dancers are Jewish, and she says so in the refusal. She does not go.
stops.quote: I would find it impossible to dance in Germany at the present time. So many artists whom I respect and admire have been persecuted, have been deprived of the right to work for ridiculous and unsatisfactory reasons, that I should consider it impossible to identify myself, by accepting the invitation, with the regime that has made such things possible. In addition, some of my concert group would not be welcomed in Germany.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, public statement declining the invitation to the dance festival of the 1936 Berlin Olympics; quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Martha Graham' citing Hanley (2004), 'The Role of Dance in the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games,' p. 136
suggested_refs: The international dance festival attached to the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games
sources: Hanley (2004), 'The Role of Dance in the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games'

stops.name: New York, American Document
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the premiere venue and day are not established by any source reached, and the pin defaults to the company's New York base rather than a named theatre
stops.campa: American Document is the first of her works to take the country itself as the material, built out of American texts read aloud between the dances. It is made in the year she turns down Berlin. Her position, given to a newspaper that summer in exactly these terms, is that a dance without national characteristics has no roots and no direct relation to life. The same year Erick Hawkins appears with the company in it, and the Roosevelt family sends for her.
stops.quote: reveal certain national characteristics because without these characteristics the dance would have no validity, no roots, no direct relation to life.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, quoted in Leah Plotkin, 'Exploring the Seven Arts,' 23 June 1938, p. 17. The Wikipedia article prefaces the sentence with its own bracketed framing, [A dance needed to]; only the quoted portion is reproduced here
suggested_refs: American Document (1938), the first of the American-subject works
sources: Leah Plotkin, 'Exploring the Seven Arts' (23 June 1938)

stops.name: The White House, Washington: the first dancer to perform there
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day of the performance is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: The Roosevelt family invites her to dance at the White House, and she becomes the first dancer to perform there. The claim is often enlarged to the first dance company; the source will not carry that, and it is left at the singular. Franklin Roosevelt is in his second term, Eleanor Roosevelt is assembling an official culture with room in it for contemporary American work, and the room being danced in had held nothing but imported repertory. Thirty-eight years later Graham comes back to this house for a medal.
suggested_refs: The White House performance of 1938, at the invitation of the Roosevelt family

stops.name: New York, Erick Hawkins joins the company
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Sources disagree and are not reconciled here: Wikipedia's 'Martha Graham' puts Hawkins joining in 1938, when he appears in American Document; Wikipedia's 'Erick Hawkins' states that in 1939 he officially joined the troupe. 1938 is the first appearance, 1939 the formal joining
stops.campa: Erick Hawkins comes out of Balanchine's American Ballet and becomes the first man to dance in Martha Graham's company. Everything she has made until now has been made on women. The vocabulary has to change to carry weight it never carried before, lifts and partnering and a second gravity on the stage. He is fifteen years younger than she is; she is forty-four the year he arrives. In 1948 she will marry him, in 1951 he will leave the company, and in 1954 the marriage ends.
suggested_refs: Erick Hawkins, first male dancer of the Martha Graham Dance Company

stops.name: Mills College, Oakland: Graham recruits Merce Cunningham
stops.date_confidence: summer 1939, the season the Bennington School of the Dance relocated west to the Mills College campus; the day is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: The Bennington summer school moves west for a season to the Mills College campus in Oakland, and Graham teaches there. Among the students is a twenty-year-old from the Cornish School in Seattle, Merce Cunningham, who has been learning her technique in Washington State for two years without ever having met her. She watches him work and asks him to come to New York. He arrives in October and dances for her six years. She is scouting for a second man in a company that a year ago had none.
suggested_refs: The 1939 Bennington School of the Dance summer session at Mills College, Oakland

stops.name: Coolidge Auditorium, Library of Congress: Appalachian Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The dance closes a four-day chamber festival held for Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge's eightieth birthday, in the auditorium she paid for inside the Library of Congress. Aaron Copland has written the score, Noguchi has built a bare porch frame and a rocking chair. Graham dances the Bride, Erick Hawkins the Husbandman, May O'Donnell the Pioneer Woman, and Merce Cunningham the Revivalist preacher, the last role she makes on him. It is wartime, and the stage holds a house going up on empty land.
stops.quote: We look at the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life, to energize the spectator into keener awareness of the vigor, the mystery, the humor, the variety, and the wonder of life.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, 'The American Dance,' in Virginia Stewart, ed., Modern Dance (1945)
suggested_refs: The Coolidge Auditorium, Library of Congress, and the Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge Foundation commissions of 1944

stops.name: New York, Merce Cunningham leaves
stops.date_confidence: January 1945; the day is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: In January Merce Cunningham leaves the company. The previous April, John Cage had played piano for his first solo concert in New York while Cunningham was still dancing for Graham by day. The divergence is not personal. Graham builds dances out of myth and psychology, out of women in the underworld reviewing their own cases, and Cunningham has stopped believing a dance needs to be about anything at all. He takes her technique with him and spends sixty years using it to argue the opposite.
suggested_refs: Merce Cunningham's departure from the Graham company, January 1945

stops.name: New York, the marriage to Erick Hawkins
stops.date_confidence: July 1948, shortly after the premiere of Night Journey; the day is not attested and no source reached names the ceremony venue within New York City
stops.campa: Shortly after Night Journey opens, in which she dances Jocasta and he dances Oedipus, Graham marries Erick Hawkins. She is fifty-four. It is her only marriage and it lasts six years. No source reached names the room they were married in. That is a blank spot in the record of a woman who documented her stage work exhaustively and gave interviews for sixty years, and it is the kind of blank spot that recurs wherever her private arrangements are concerned. What survives in print is the stage version, Jocasta and Oedipus.
suggested_refs: Night Journey (1947), the Jocasta work whose premiere precedes the marriage

stops.name: New York, Hawkins leaves the company
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Hawkins leaves the company after thirteen years in it. He has begun making his own work along lines she does not accept, toward ease and released weight rather than tension, and there is no room in her studio for a second choreographer. The marriage survives the departure by three years on paper. The divorce is granted in 1954. She does not marry again and does not, in anything she publishes afterwards, discuss what happened between them off the stage.
suggested_refs: Erick Hawkins's departure, 1951, and the divorce of 1954

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Manhattan: the Pilates mats
stops.date_confidence: 1953 is the year given for Ron Fletcher's arrival at the studio; the month is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Ron Fletcher, a principal in Graham's company, walks into Joseph Pilates's gymnasium on Eighth Avenue with an injury and stays. Pilates is a German boxer and self-taught body mechanic, interned on the Isle of Man in the first war, who has been rebuilding American dancers ever since. George Balanchine sends his own injured to the same mats. The two studios disagree about everything a dance can be, and both of them owe their working knees to one room off Columbus Circle.
suggested_refs: Joseph Pilates's studio at 939 Eighth Avenue, shared clinic of the Graham and Balanchine companies

stops.name: Adelphi Theatre, Manhattan: Clytemnestra
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The house at 152 West 54th Street was still the Adelphi on the premiere night and was renamed the 54th Street Theatre later in 1958; most accounts of the premiere give the later name, which is anachronistic
stops.campa: Clytemnestra fills an evening, the first American modern dance work to do so, and it is built on a queen reviewing her own case in the underworld. Halim El-Dabh, an Egyptian composer, writes the score. Graham is sixty-three and dancing the title role. The Greek material has been entering her work for a decade, Jocasta and Medea and Ariadne, and here it takes the whole stage: a woman who murdered and was murdered, going through the evidence in a place where no verdict can be revised.
suggested_refs: Clytemnestra (1958), score by Halim El-Dabh, premiered at the Adelphi Theatre, 152 West 54th Street

stops.name: Odeon of Herodes Atticus, Athens: the touring stages
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The company's own history page names the Odeon among its landmark stages but gives no year and no tour itinerary, and the claim could not be cross-checked against a dated source. The 1960 anchor is a placeholder inside the touring decades, not an attested date. The same page names the Great Pyramids at Giza, the Paris Opera and Covent Garden with no dates either
stops.campa: The company dances on the stone of a Roman theatre built in the second century on the south slope of the Acropolis, under the rock where the Oresteia was first performed. The woman who made Clytemnestra brings her back to the hill she came off. In the same undated stretch of touring the company performs before the pyramids at Giza, at the Paris Opera, and at Covent Garden. Its own history lists the venues and supplies no year for any of them, so the tours survive as a list of stones and not as an itinerary.
stops.quote: The most brilliant scientific discoveries will in time change and perhaps grow obsolete as new scientific manifestations emerge. But art is eternal, for it reveals the inner landscape, which is the soul of man.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, 'I Am a Dancer' (1952), reprinted in The Routledge Dance Studies Reader (1998). Wikiquote files the passage under a This I Believe broadcast, but the This I Believe archive publishes Graham's essay as 'An Athlete of God' and that text does not contain this sentence, so the broadcast attribution is dropped
suggested_refs: The Odeon of Herodes Atticus, Athens, named among the company's landmark stages

stops.name: New York, the death of Louis Horst
stops.date_confidence: 1964 is the year given for Horst's death in the framing of the Wikipedia article; the month is not established by any source reached, and the tribute quoted is not dated within that year
stops.campa: Louis Horst dies. He had been Denishawn's musical director when Graham was a student there, came east when she did, played and composed for the self-financed concerts of the twenties, and stayed beside her through the decades in which the audience for this work had to be assembled one recital at a time. She is seventy. She has outlived the man who believed in the technique before there was any evidence for it, and what she writes for him is one sentence about what his faith gave her.
stops.quote: His sympathy and understanding, but primarily his faith, gave me a landscape to move in.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham on Louis Horst, quoted in Russell Freedman, Martha Graham: A Dancer's Life (Clarion Books, 1998), p. 134
suggested_refs: Louis Horst, musical director of Denishawn and composer for the early Graham concerts
sources: Russell Freedman, Martha Graham: A Dancer's Life (1998)

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the founding of Batsheva
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Bethsabée de Rothschild, who has been funding Graham's company in New York, founds a dance company in Tel Aviv on Christmas Eve and gives it her own name. Graham is its artistic adviser. She hands over seven of her existing works outright and choreographs one new piece for it. Israeli modern dance begins with an American technique installed whole, by a French banking heiress, in a state sixteen years old. Graham is seventy and has never lived in the country whose dancers now start from her syllabus.
suggested_refs: The Batsheva Dance Company, founded 24 December 1964 by Bethsabée de Rothschild

segments.name: The Last Performance and the Return

stops.name: New York, Cortege of Eagles: the last performance
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The year is disputed and is not resolved here. Graham herself listed her final performance as her 1970 appearance in Cortege of Eagles at the age of seventy-six, and her own reckoning is used as the anchor; other accounts give 1968 or 1969
stops.campa: She dances for the last time at seventy-six, in Cortege of Eagles, and she does not choose the moment. The body ends the argument for her. She has been on a stage since 1916, fifty-four years, and has made every role she ever danced on her own frame. What follows is not administration. It is a collapse. The dances go on being performed in front of her by younger women, in costumes cut to her measurements, to counts she invented and taught them herself.
stops.quote: It wasn't until years after I had relinquished a ballet that I could bear to watch someone else dance it... I think that is a circle of hell Dante omitted.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, Blood Memory: An Autobiography (Doubleday, 1991), p. 237
suggested_refs: Cortege of Eagles (1967), the work of her final appearance as a dancer

stops.name: New York, the years without dancing
stops.date_confidence: the collapse runs from the end of her performing career to her hospitalization and recovery; 1971 is an anchor inside that stretch and not an attested date
stops.campa: She stops going to the studio. She drinks, refuses visitors, eats almost nothing, and is eventually hospitalized. The company she built continues without her and comes close to folding. She is in her late seventies and has been the working discipline of her own institution for forty-five years, and the institution finds it does not know how to be an institution with her out of the room. She sets all of this down in her own book afterwards without arranging it into a lesson.
stops.quote: I had lost my will to live. I stayed home alone, ate very little, and drank too much and brooded.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, Blood Memory: An Autobiography (1991), p. 237
suggested_refs: The account of the post-retirement collapse in Blood Memory, p. 237

stops.name: New York, the return to the studio
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: She stops drinking, comes back to the studio, and reorganizes the company from the outside, as a director who will never again appear on the stage she is directing. Ten more ballets follow in the years after. She is seventy-eight when she begins again and keeps choreographing for eighteen more years, longer than most dance careers run from first class to last curtain. Nothing made in the second half is danced by her, and she has said in print that the watching is the hard part.
suggested_refs: The reorganized Martha Graham Dance Company after 1972

stops.name: The White House, Washington: the Presidential Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day of the ceremony is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Gerald Ford gives her the Presidential Medal of Freedom and calls her a national treasure. Thirty-eight years earlier she had danced in this house as the first dancer ever to do so, for a president in his second term with a war on its way. She is eighty-two. The National Medal of Arts follows in 1985 and the Samuel H. Scripps award, presented by Betty Ford, in 1981. The republic that had no use whatever for her rented recitals in 1926 has, inside one lifetime, made her official.
suggested_refs: The Presidential Medal of Freedom of 1976, conferred by Gerald Ford

stops.name: Kennedy Center, Washington: the Honors
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day of the ceremony is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: She receives a Kennedy Center Honor in the award's second year, in a class with Aaron Copland, who wrote Appalachian Spring for her thirty-five years earlier, and with Ella Fitzgerald, Henry Fonda, and Tennessee Williams. The inaugural class, the year before, had been Marian Anderson, Fred Astaire, George Balanchine, Richard Rodgers, and Arthur Rubinstein. She is regularly written into that first list by people who assume she has to have been in it.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy Center Honors class of 1979

stops.name: Paris, the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the day is not, and no source reached names the ceremony venue within Paris. The city itself is well attested
stops.campa: Jack Lang, minister of culture, awards her the Legion of Honour. France has been conferring the order since Napoleon and confers it here on an American who taught European dancers to put their weight into the floor rather than lift it off. No source reached names the room or the day within the city. She is ninety years old and still directing a company and still putting new work on a stage, so the Paris decoration arrives in the middle of a working life rather than at the end of one.
suggested_refs: The Legion of Honour conferred by Jack Lang, minister of culture, 1984

stops.name: New York, the interview at ninety
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of publication
stops.campa: The New York Times sends a reporter to her studio six weeks before her ninety-first birthday. She is still running the company and still making new work. In the same conversation she says that the only sin is mediocrity, and that line gets painted onto studio walls for the next forty years. She also says that the body says what words cannot. That one circulates almost everywhere with its middle silently removed, two separated statements pushed into one.
stops.quote: To me, the body says what words cannot. ... Dance is the hidden language of the soul, of the body.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham, 'Martha Graham Reflects on Her Art and a Life in Dance,' The New York Times, 31 March 1985; republished in The New York Times Guide to the Arts of the 20th Century (2002), p. 2734. The two sentences are separated in the original by intervening text about dance as the first art; the ellipsis marks that omission
suggested_refs: 'Martha Graham Reflects on Her Art and a Life in Dance,' New York Times, 31 March 1985

stops.name: New York, Maple Leaf Rag
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the premiere day is not established by any source reached
stops.campa: Her last completed ballet is set to Scott Joplin. She is ninety-six years old. It is the hundred and eighty-first work of a life by the count usually given, a figure that no source reached has itemized against a surviving repertory, and many of the earlier works are lost or were never fixed in any recoverable form. She has been at this for sixty-four years, since renting the 48th Street Theatre with her own money and putting eighteen short dances on it in one evening.
suggested_refs: Maple Leaf Rag (1990), the last completed Graham ballet

stops.name: New York, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: She dies of pneumonia in New York on the first of April, ninety-six years old, with a new piece planned and not begun. No source reached this session names the hospital, the residence, or the neighbourhood. She had been making dances in this city since 1926, when the entire audience for what she did consisted of the people she could persuade to buy a ticket to one evening in a Broadway house she was paying for out of her own pocket. The company she left behind is by then the oldest in the country.
suggested_refs: The Martha Graham Dance Company, at her death the oldest dance company in America

stops.name: Sangre de Cristo Mountains, New Mexico: the ashes
stops.date_confidence: the scattering is attested; no date and no coordinates are published. The pin is a midpoint of a range running roughly from Santa Fe to Taos, and the June anchor is a placeholder after the April death
stops.campa: There is no grave. Her ashes are scattered over the Sangre de Cristo mountains in northern New Mexico, high dry country she never set a dance in. One account of the scattering makes the range her source material, which no source reached supports: Frontier and Appalachian Spring evoke an American West that is nowhere in particular, a rail fence and a porch frame and open ground behind them. The actual mountains take her. The company goes on performing the invented ones.
suggested_refs: The Sangre de Cristo range of northern New Mexico, between Santa Fe and Taos

stops.name: New York, Blood Memory published
stops.date_confidence: published in the autumn of 1991, months after her death; the month anchor is approximate
stops.campa: Blood Memory is finished weeks before her final illness and published that autumn. It ends with her own account of the drinking and the depression, which she puts in the book rather than leaving to the biographers. The passage everyone quotes is not in it. She said that to Agnes de Mille, who printed it in her own life of Graham the same year, and it has circulated ever since as a description of Graham rather than as instructions Graham gave to somebody else.
stops.quote: There is a vitality, a life force, an energy, a quickening that is translated through you into action, and because there is only one of you in all of time, this expression is unique. ... No artist is pleased. ... There is only a queer divine dissatisfaction, a blessed unrest that keeps us marching and makes us more alive than the others.
stops.quote_source: Martha Graham to Agnes de Mille, quoted in Agnes de Mille, Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham (Random House, 1991), p. 264. Ellipses mark omissions in the passage as printed
suggested_refs: Blood Memory: An Autobiography (Doubleday, 1991), published posthumously
sources: Agnes de Mille, Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham (1991)

stops.name: United States District Court, Southern District of New York: who owns a dance
stops.date_confidence: the Southern District ruled on 7 August 2001 and again on 23 August 2002, with a further ruling on 23 June 2005; the ownership holding is anchored here to the 2002 decision
stops.campa: Her will leaves the rights over her choreography to Ron Protas, her companion and heir. The board dismisses him in 2000 and he sues to stop the company dancing her dances. Judge Miriam Goldman Cedarbaum holds that Graham did not personally own most of the work: she made it as an employee of the institution carrying her name. The company recovers all but two of the dances at issue, wins again in the Second Circuit in 2004, and performs a full season for the first time since the suit began.
suggested_refs: Martha Graham School and Dance Foundation v. Martha Graham Center, S.D.N.Y. 2002 and 2d Cir. 2004 (380 F.3d 624)
sources: CourtListener docket, Martha Graham School v. Martha Graham Center

stops.name: Library for the Performing Arts, Lincoln Center: the archive
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, the announcement being timed to her birthday
stops.campa: On what would have been her hundred and twenty-sixth birthday, the New York Public Library announces that Graham's personal archive has come to the Jerome Robbins Dance Division: papers, photographs, her script for Night Journey, handwritten notes for American Document, and film of her dancing in Appalachian Spring and Hérodiade. Nine years earlier, on the same date, Google had replaced its homepage logo worldwide with a drawing of her. The technique is taught on every continent; the woman is now a collection.
suggested_refs: The Martha Graham archive, Jerome Robbins Dance Division, New York Public Library for the Performing Arts
sources: Wikipedia, 'Martha Graham', citing the NYPL announcement
